html:
Tansen was the most famous musician of India, a singer at the court of the Mughal emperor Akbar. The classical music of north India traces its line back to him.

He was born about 1500 near Gwalior, then a great centre of music, and is said to have studied with the holy man Swami Haridas of Vrindavan. He spent most of his life at the court of the king of Rewa. In 1562 Akbar, hearing of him, had him sent to Agra. He was already about sixty. Akbar gave him 200,000 rupees after his first performance and counted him among the nine "jewels" of the court.

He sang dhrupad, a slow and grand style, and several ragas still played are credited to him, among them Miyan ki Todi, Miyan ki Malhar and Darbari. Abul Fazl wrote that India had not seen a singer like him for a thousand years.

The stories outgrew the man. One raga, sung by him, is said to have lit the palace lamps; another brought rain.

He died in 1589 and is buried at Gwalior, where a music festival is held at his tomb every year. Families of musicians who claim descent from him or his pupils carried the tradition on.
